summary.text: A finite computation of the recurrence at \(n=20\) shows that \(13^2\mid a(20)\). Since \(13\) is coprime to both 2 and 3, any factorization \(a(20)=2^r3^s m\) would force \(13^2\mid m\), contradicting that \(m\) is squarefree.

full_proof.text:
Let \(d(x)\) denote the number of decimal digits of a nonnegative integer \(x\), with the convention \(d(0)=1\). If \(x\Vert y\) denotes the decimal concatenation of \(x\) followed by \(y\), then
\[
 x\Vert y=x10^{d(y)}+y.
\]
Thus the sequence is defined by
\[
a(1)=0,\qquad a(2)=1,
\]
and, for \(n\geq 3\),
\[
 a(n)=\left|(a(n-1)\Vert a(n-2))-(a(n-2)\Vert a(n-1))\right|.
\]
We will disprove the proposed squarefree-factor assertion at \(n=20\).

For convenient computation, put
\[
 x=a(n-1),\qquad y=a(n-2),\qquad
 D_n=(x\Vert y)-(y\Vert x).
\]
Expanding the two concatenations gives
\[
 D_n=x10^{d(y)}+y-y10^{d(x)}-x
     =x\bigl(10^{d(y)}-1\bigr)-y\bigl(10^{d(x)}-1\bigr),                 \tag{1}
\]
and \(a(n)=|D_n|\).

We compute through \(n=20\), retaining residues modulo
\[
13^2=169.
\]
The following table contains all the data needed for the computation. In the table, \(d_n=d(a(n))\), \(r_n\) is the least nonnegative residue of \(a(n)\) modulo \(169\), and the sign is the sign of the signed difference \(D_n\). The last two columns, for \(n\geq3\), are
\[
 P_n=10^{d(a(n-2))}\pmod{169},\qquad
 Q_n=10^{d(a(n-1))}\pmod{169}.
\]

\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|c|r|r}
 n&d_n&r_n&\operatorname{sign}(D_n)&P_n&Q_n\\ \hline
 1&1&0&-&-&-\\
 2&1&1&-&-&-\\
 3&1&9&+&10&10\\
 4&2&72&+&10&10\\
 5&3&74&-&10&100\\
 6&5&44&-&100&155\\
 7&8&93&+&155&121\\
 8&13&112&-&121&165\\
 9&19&98&+&165&23\\
10&32&147&+&23&114\\
11&51&98&-&114&87\\
12&83&27&-&87&116\\
13&133&133&+&116&121\\
14&216&26&+&121&153\\
15&349&39&-&153&92\\
16&565&65&-&92&49\\
17&913&104&-&49&114\\
18&1478&13&+&114&153\\
19&2391&39&-&153&35\\
20&3869&0&-&35&116
\end{array}
\]

Here is how this finite table is obtained and checked. Starting with \(0\) and \(1\), one applies (1), takes the absolute value, counts the resulting decimal digits, and reduces modulo \(169\). The first several calculations, displayed exactly, are
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(3)&=|10-1|=9,\\
a(4)&=|9\Vert1-1\Vert9|=|91-19|=72,\\
a(5)&=|72\Vert9-9\Vert72|=|729-972|=243,\\
a(6)&=|243\Vert72-72\Vert243|=|24372-72243|=47871,\\
a(7)&=23523372,\\
a(8)&=2434786275501.
\end{aligned}
\]
These agree with the digit lengths and residues in the table: for example, \(243\equiv74\pmod{169}\) and \(47871\equiv44\pmod{169}\).

For every subsequent row, if the preceding two residues are known, equation (1) gives
\[
 D_n\equiv r_{n-1}(P_n-1)-r_{n-2}(Q_n-1)\pmod{169}.                 \tag{2}
\]
If the sign in the table is positive, this is the residue of \(a(n)\); if the sign is negative, its negative is the residue of \(a(n)\). The digit counts and signs are obtained at the same time by ordinary decimal evaluation of the two concatenations. Thus, for instance, the entry \(d_n=k\) asserts the directly checked inequalities
\(10^{k-1}\leq a(n)<10^k\), and the sign column records the direct comparison of \(a(n-1)\Vert a(n-2)\) with \(a(n-2)\Vert a(n-1)\). No factorization of the enormous terms is needed.

As illustrations of the modular induction, for \(n=5\) we have \(r_4=72\), \(r_3=9\), \(P_5=10\), and \(Q_5=100\). Hence
\[
D_5\equiv72(10-1)-9(100-1)=-243\pmod{169}.
\]
Since \(D_5<0\), this gives \(a(5)\equiv243\equiv74\pmod{169}\), as recorded. Each following line is obtained in exactly the same way, using repeated squaring or repeated multiplication by \(10\) to calculate the two displayed powers modulo \(169\).

Most importantly, the final line can be checked immediately from the preceding data. We have
\[
 a(19)\equiv39\pmod{169},\qquad a(18)\equiv13\pmod{169},
\]
while
\[
 d(a(18))=1478,\qquad d(a(19))=2391,
\]
and
\[
10^{1478}\equiv35\pmod{169},\qquad
10^{2391}\equiv116\pmod{169}.
\]
Substitution in (2) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{20}
 &\equiv39(35-1)-13(116-1)\pmod{169}\\
 &=39\cdot34-13\cdot115\\
 &=1326-1495\\
 &=-169\\
 &\equiv0\pmod{169}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking an absolute value does not affect divisibility. Therefore
\[
169=13^2\mid a(20).                                                     \tag{3}
\]

Now suppose, contrary to what we will prove, that the proposed conclusion holds at \(n=20\). Then there are nonnegative integers \(r,s\) and a squarefree nonnegative integer \(m\) such that
\[
 a(20)=2^r3^s m.                                                        \tag{4}
\]
(The divisibility-by-\(3\) part of the conjecture is irrelevant here; to refute the conjunction it suffices to refute this asserted representation.)

The number \(169\) is relatively prime to both \(2\) and \(3\), because its only prime divisor is \(13\). It follows that
\[
\gcd(169,2^r3^s)=1.
\]
Combining (3) and (4), we have
\[
169\mid 2^r3^s m.
\]
Coprime cancellation now gives
\[
169\mid m.                                                             \tag{5}
\]
For completeness, this cancellation follows directly from Bézout's identity: since \(169\) and \(2^r3^s\) are coprime, there exist integers \(u,v\) such that
\[
169u+2^r3^s v=1.
\]
Multiplying by \(m\), both terms on the left are divisible by \(169\): the first visibly, and the second because \(169\mid2^r3^s m\). Hence \(169\mid m\).

But (5) says precisely that the square of the nonunit prime \(13\) divides \(m\). This contradicts squarefreeness: a squarefree integer has no square of a prime as a divisor (equivalently, whenever \(t^2\mid m\), the divisor \(t\) must be a unit). Here \(13^2\mid m\), while \(13\neq1\) and hence \(13\) is not a unit among the nonnegative integers.

Thus \(a(20)\) cannot be written as \(2^r3^s m\) with \(m\) squarefree. Since \(20>2\), this is a counterexample to the universal conjecture. Therefore the conjecture is false.
